Stochastic Optimal Control

Introduction¶

Stochastic optimal control (SOC) is the mathematical theory of making sequential decisions in systems whose state evolves stochastically over time. The agent observes the current state of the system, applies a control, and the system transitions to a new state according to a stochastic law. The goal is to choose a sequence of controls — a policy — that minimises an expected cumulative cost over a finite or infinite horizon. SOC extends classical optimal control theory, which addresses deterministic systems, to the regime where the state dynamics are driven by random processes such as the Wiener process introduced in chapter Stochastic Calculus.

The mathematical tools developed in this chapter provide the foundation for two distinct classes of trading problems addressed later in this book: optimal execution scheduling (chapter Optimal Execution Theory) and optimal market making (chapter Optimal Market Making). In the execution problem, the agent must liquidate an inventory at minimum expected cost while controlling timing risk; the state is the remaining inventory and the control is the trading rate. In the market making problem, the agent must quote bid and ask prices dynamically to maximise expected profit while managing inventory risk; the state is the inventory and the control is the spread quoted around the mid-price. Despite the different economic contexts, both problems share the same mathematical structure: a stochastic dynamical system, a cost functional, and a backward equation — the Bellman equation in discrete time, or the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation in continuous time — that determines the value of the optimal policy at each state and time.

The chapter is organised as follows. We begin with discrete-time dynamic programming (Dynamic programming in discrete time), which introduces Bellman’s principle of optimality and the backward induction algorithm in the simplest setting. We then extend to continuous-time control (The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation), where the state follows a stochastic differential equation and the optimal value function satisfies the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation. We next present the variational approach (The variational approach), which simplifies the optimisation to an ordinary differential equation when the stochastic noise enters the cost functional only through the trajectory of the state — a structure that appears in the Almgren–Chriss model. Finally, we derive the Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control (LQSC) framework (Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control), which yields closed-form solutions via Riccati equations and is the method of choice for execution and market making problems with quadratic cost structures.

Dynamic programming in discrete time¶

Problem setup¶

We consider a system evolving over discrete time steps k=0,1,…,Nk = 0, 1, \ldots, Nk=0,1,…,N, where NNN is the terminal time. At each step kkk the system is in state xk∈X⊆Rnx_k \in \mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^nxk​∈X⊆Rn and the agent selects a control uk∈U(xk)⊆Rmu_k \in \mathcal{U}(x_k) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^muk​∈U(xk​)⊆Rm from a feasible set that may depend on the current state. The state then transitions according to the dynamics

xk+1=fk(xk,uk,wk)x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k)xk+1​=fk​(xk​,uk​,wk​)
(1)

where wkw_kwk​ is an exogenous random disturbance with known distribution that is independent of the past history of states and controls. Applying control uku_kuk​ in state xkx_kxk​ incurs a running cost ck(xk,uk)c_k(x_k, u_k)ck​(xk​,uk​), and reaching terminal state xNx_NxN​ incurs a terminal cost ψ(xN)\psi(x_N)ψ(xN​). The total cost of a sequence of controls u=(u0,u1,…,uN−1)\mathbf{u} = (u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_{N-1})u=(u0​,u1​,…,uN−1​) is

J(u)=∑k=0N−1ck(xk,uk)+ψ(xN)J(\mathbf{u}) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(x_k, u_k) + \psi(x_N)J(u)=k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​,uk​)+ψ(xN​)
(2)

This is a random variable because the state trajectory (x0,x1,…,xN)(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N)(x0​,x1​,…,xN​) depends on the random disturbances (w0,w1,…,wN−1)(w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_{N-1})(w0​,w1​,…,wN−1​). The objective is to find a policy π=(π0,π1,…,πN−1)\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_{N-1})π=(π0​,π1​,…,πN−1​), where πk:X→U\pi_k: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{U}πk​:X→U maps states to controls, that minimises the expected total cost:

min⁡π E[∑k=0N−1ck(xk,πk(xk))+ψ(xN) ∣ x0]\min_\pi \, \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(x_k, \pi_k(x_k)) + \psi(x_N) \,\Big|\, x_0\right]πmin​E[k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​,πk​(xk​))+ψ(xN​)∣∣​x0​]
(3)

A policy of this form — mapping the state to a control at each step — is called a feedback or closed-loop policy. The key result of dynamic programming is that the optimal policy has exactly this feedback structure: the optimal action at each step depends only on the current state, not on the full history of states and controls.

Bellman’s principle of optimality¶

The core insight behind dynamic programming is Bellman’s principle of optimality: the tail of an optimal policy is itself optimal. Formally, if (u0∗,u1∗,…,uN−1∗)(u_0^*, u_1^*, \ldots, u_{N-1}^*)(u0∗​,u1∗​,…,uN−1∗​) is an optimal policy, then for any intermediate time kkk and any state xkx_kxk​ reachable under the optimal policy, (uk∗,uk+1∗,…,uN−1∗)(u_k^*, u_{k+1}^*, \ldots, u_{N-1}^*)(uk∗​,uk+1∗​,…,uN−1∗​) is an optimal policy for the sub-problem starting at time kkk in state xkx_kxk​.

This principle justifies decomposing the global optimisation into a sequence of local optimisations, solved backwards from the terminal time.

The Bellman equation¶

Define the value function Vk(x)V_k(x)Vk​(x) as the minimum expected cost achievable from state xxx at time kkk:

Vk(x)=min⁡πk,…,πN−1E[∑j=kN−1cj(xj,πj(xj))+ψ(xN) ∣ xk=x]V_k(x) = \min_{\pi_k, \ldots, \pi_{N-1}} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j=k}^{N-1} c_j(x_j, \pi_j(x_j)) + \psi(x_N) \,\Big|\, x_k = x\right]Vk​(x)=πk​,…,πN−1​min​E⎣⎡​j=k∑N−1​cj​(xj​,πj​(xj​))+ψ(xN​)∣∣​xk​=x⎦⎤​
(4)

The terminal value function is simply the terminal cost: VN(x)=ψ(x)V_N(x) = \psi(x)VN​(x)=ψ(x).

By the principle of optimality, applying the optimal first action uk∗u_k^*uk∗​ and then following the optimal policy from the resulting state xk+1x_{k+1}xk+1​ gives:

Vk(x)=min⁡u∈U(x)Ewk[ck(x,u)+Vk+1(fk(x,u,wk))]\boxed{V_k(x) = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\left[c_k(x, u) + V_{k+1}(f_k(x, u, w_k))\right]}Vk​(x)=u∈U(x)min​Ewk​​[ck​(x,u)+Vk+1​(fk​(x,u,wk​))]​
(5)

with VN(x)=ψ(x)V_N(x) = \psi(x)VN​(x)=ψ(x). This is the Bellman equation (or dynamic programming equation). It reduces the optimisation over sequences of controls into a sequence of single-step optimisations, each requiring only the value function at the next step. The optimal policy at step kkk is recovered from the minimiser:

πk∗(x)=arg⁡min⁡u∈U(x)Ewk[ck(x,u)+Vk+1(fk(x,u,wk))]\pi_k^*(x) = \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\left[c_k(x, u) + V_{k+1}(f_k(x, u, w_k))\right]πk∗​(x)=argu∈U(x)min​Ewk​​[ck​(x,u)+Vk+1​(fk​(x,u,wk​))]
(6)

Backward induction algorithm¶

The Bellman equation defines a backward induction algorithm for computing the optimal value function and policy:

  1. Initialise: set VN(x)=ψ(x)V_N(x) = \psi(x)VN​(x)=ψ(x) for all states xxx.

  2. For k=N−1,N−2,…,0k = N-1, N-2, \ldots, 0k=N−1,N−2,…,0:

    • For each state x∈Xx \in \mathcal{X}x∈X, compute:

      Vk(x)=min⁡u∈U(x)Ewk[ck(x,u)+Vk+1(fk(x,u,wk))]V_k(x) = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}(x)} \mathbb{E}_{w_k}\left[c_k(x, u) + V_{k+1}(f_k(x, u, w_k))\right]Vk​(x)=u∈U(x)min​Ewk​​[ck​(x,u)+Vk+1​(fk​(x,u,wk​))]
      (7)

    • Record the minimiser as πk∗(x)\pi_k^*(x)πk∗​(x).

The algorithm sweeps backwards from the terminal time, propagating value information from the future into the current decision. Once all VkV_kVk​ and πk∗\pi_k^*πk∗​ are computed, the optimal forward trajectory is obtained by simulating the system under π∗\pi^*π∗ from x0x_0x0​.

The feasibility of the algorithm depends on the structure of the problem. When X\mathcal{X}X is finite and small, the expectation and minimisation can be computed explicitly. When X\mathcal{X}X is continuous, the value function is defined over an uncountable domain, and special structure must be exploited to obtain tractable solutions. The LQSC framework in Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control provides one such tractable case.

Example: discrete inventory liquidation¶

Consider a trader who must sell XXX shares over NNN time periods. Let the state be the remaining inventory xk∈{0,1,…,X}x_k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, X\}xk​∈{0,1,…,X} and the control be the number of shares sold in period kkk: uk∈{0,1,…,xk}u_k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, x_k\}uk​∈{0,1,…,xk​}. The inventory dynamics are xk+1=xk−ukx_{k+1} = x_k - u_kxk+1​=xk​−uk​ (deterministic, no noise). The price in period kkk is SkS_kSk​ and the execution price is Pk=Sk−ηukP_k = S_k - \eta u_kPk​=Sk​−ηuk​ (linear temporary impact). Suppose the price evolves as Sk+1=Sk+ϵk+1S_{k+1} = S_k + \epsilon_{k+1}Sk+1​=Sk​+ϵk+1​ with ϵk\epsilon_kϵk​ i.i.d. zero-mean noise.

The total proceeds are ∑k=0N−1ukPk=∑k=0N−1uk(Sk−ηuk)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} u_k P_k = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} u_k (S_k - \eta u_k)∑k=0N−1​uk​Pk​=∑k=0N−1​uk​(Sk​−ηuk​), and we impose the constraint ∑k=0N−1uk=X\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} u_k = X∑k=0N−1​uk​=X (all shares must be sold). The expected total proceeds are:

E[∑k=0N−1ukSk−η∑k=0N−1uk2]\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} u_k S_k - \eta \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} u_k^2\right]E[k=0∑N−1​uk​Sk​−ηk=0∑N−1​uk2​]
(8)

Since prices follow a martingale (E[Sk]=S0\mathbb{E}[S_k] = S_0E[Sk​]=S0​) and the inventory xk=X−∑j<kujx_k = X - \sum_{j<k} u_jxk​=X−∑j<k​uj​ is determined by prior decisions, this problem has quadratic structure. Bertsimas and Lo Bertsimas & Lo, 1998 show that the optimal policy under this formulation distributes the remaining inventory equally at each step: uk∗=xk/(N−k)u_k^* = x_k / (N - k)uk∗​=xk​/(N−k), recovering the TWAP schedule. The value function is quadratic in the state, a structure that carries over to the continuous-time case and the LQSC framework.

The Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation¶

From discrete to continuous time¶

The discrete-time Bellman equation can be extended to continuous time by taking the step size Δt→0\Delta t \to 0Δt→0. Consider the state dynamics

dXt=μ(Xt,ut,t) dt+σ(Xt,t) dWtdX_t = \mu(X_t, u_t, t) \, dt + \sigma(X_t, t) \, dW_tdXt​=μ(Xt​,ut​,t)dt+σ(Xt​,t)dWt​
(9)

where WtW_tWt​ is a standard Wiener process (see chapter Stochastic Calculus), and the running cost c(t,Xt,ut) dtc(t, X_t, u_t) \, dtc(t,Xt​,ut​)dt is incurred continuously. The state is Xt∈RnX_t \in \mathbb{R}^nXt​∈Rn, the control is ut∈Uu_t \in \mathcal{U}ut​∈U, and the drift μ\muμ is allowed to depend on the control while the volatility σ\sigmaσ does not (for simplicity; this restriction can be relaxed). The value function is defined as:

J(t,x)=min⁡{us}t≤s≤TE[∫tTc(s,Xs,us) ds+ψ(XT) ∣ Xt=x]J(t, x) = \min_{\{u_s\}_{t \leq s \leq T}} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_t^T c(s, X_s, u_s) \, ds + \psi(X_T) \,\Bigg|\, X_t = x\right]J(t,x)={us​}t≤s≤T​min​E[∫tT​c(s,Xs​,us​)ds+ψ(XT​)∣∣​Xt​=x]
(10)

and satisfies J(T,x)=ψ(x)J(T, x) = \psi(x)J(T,x)=ψ(x). We seek the partial differential equation (PDE) that JJJ satisfies for t<Tt < Tt<T.

HJB derivation¶

Applying the Bellman principle over the short interval [t,t+dt][t, t + dt][t,t+dt]:

J(t,x)=min⁡u∈U E[c(t,x,u) dt+J(t+dt,Xt+dt) ∣ Xt=x]J(t, x) = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \, \mathbb{E}\left[c(t, x, u) \, dt + J(t + dt, X_{t+dt}) \,\Big|\, X_t = x\right]J(t,x)=u∈Umin​E[c(t,x,u)dt+J(t+dt,Xt+dt​)∣∣​Xt​=x]
(11)

Using Ito’s lemma (chapter Stochastic Calculus, Paragraph) to expand J(t+dt,Xt+dt)J(t + dt, X_{t+dt})J(t+dt,Xt+dt​):

J(t+dt,Xt+dt)=J(t,x)+∂J∂tdt+∂J∂xdXt+12∂2J∂x2(dXt)2J(t + dt, X_{t+dt}) = J(t, x) + \frac{\partial J}{\partial t} dt + \frac{\partial J}{\partial x} dX_t + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 J}{\partial x^2} (dX_t)^2J(t+dt,Xt+dt​)=J(t,x)+∂t∂J​dt+∂x∂J​dXt​+21​∂x2∂2J​(dXt​)2
(12)

Taking expectations and using (dXt)2=σ2(x,t) dt(dX_t)^2 = \sigma^2(x,t) \, dt(dXt​)2=σ2(x,t)dt and E[dWt]=0\mathbb{E}[dW_t] = 0E[dWt​]=0:

E[J(t+dt,Xt+dt)∣Xt=x]=J(t,x)+(∂J∂t+μ(x,u,t)∂J∂x+12σ2(x,t)∂2J∂x2)dt\mathbb{E}[J(t+dt, X_{t+dt}) | X_t = x] = J(t,x) + \left(\frac{\partial J}{\partial t} + \mu(x, u, t) \frac{\partial J}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(x,t) \frac{\partial^2 J}{\partial x^2}\right) dtE[J(t+dt,Xt+dt​)∣Xt​=x]=J(t,x)+(∂t∂J​+μ(x,u,t)∂x∂J​+21​σ2(x,t)∂x2∂2J​)dt
(13)

Substituting back into the Bellman equation and rearranging:

−∂J∂t=min⁡u∈U[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)∂J∂x+12σ2(x,t)∂2J∂x2]\boxed{-\frac{\partial J}{\partial t} = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \left[c(t, x, u) + \mu(x, u, t) \frac{\partial J}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(x,t) \frac{\partial^2 J}{\partial x^2}\right]}−∂t∂J​=u∈Umin​[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)∂x∂J​+21​σ2(x,t)∂x2∂2J​]​
(14)

with terminal condition J(T,x)=ψ(x)J(T, x) = \psi(x)J(T,x)=ψ(x). This is the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation. It is a nonlinear PDE running backwards in time from the terminal condition. The optimal control u∗(t,x)u^*(t,x)u∗(t,x) is the minimiser of the right-hand side at each (t,x)(t,x)(t,x):

u∗(t,x)=arg⁡min⁡u∈U[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)∂J∂x]u^*(t, x) = \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \left[c(t, x, u) + \mu(x, u, t) \frac{\partial J}{\partial x}\right]u∗(t,x)=argu∈Umin​[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)∂x∂J​]
(15)

Once the HJB PDE is solved for JJJ and the optimal control u∗u^*u∗ is obtained in feedback form, the optimal policy generates the optimal state trajectory by forward simulation under u∗(t,Xt)u^*(t, X_t)u∗(t,Xt​).

For multivariate states Xt∈RnX_t \in \mathbb{R}^nXt​∈Rn driven by a multivariate Wiener process Wt∈RdW_t \in \mathbb{R}^dWt​∈Rd, with dynamics dXt=μ(Xt,ut,t) dt+Σ(Xt,t) dWtdX_t = \mu(X_t, u_t, t) \, dt + \Sigma(X_t, t) \, dW_tdXt​=μ(Xt​,ut​,t)dt+Σ(Xt​,t)dWt​, the HJB equation generalises to:

−∂J∂t=min⁡u∈U[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)T∇xJ+12tr(ΣΣT∇xx2J)]-\frac{\partial J}{\partial t} = \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \left[c(t, x, u) + \mu(x, u, t)^T \nabla_x J + \frac{1}{2} \text{tr}\left(\Sigma \Sigma^T \nabla_{xx}^2 J\right)\right]−∂t∂J​=u∈Umin​[c(t,x,u)+μ(x,u,t)T∇x​J+21​tr(ΣΣT∇xx2​J)]
(16)

where ∇xJ\nabla_x J∇x​J is the gradient vector and ∇xx2J\nabla_{xx}^2 J∇xx2​J is the Hessian matrix of JJJ with respect to xxx.

Terminal conditions and boundary conditions¶

The HJB equation is solved backwards from the terminal condition J(T,x)=ψ(x)J(T, x) = \psi(x)J(T,x)=ψ(x), which encodes the terminal cost at the end of the horizon. For execution problems, the most common terminal cost is a large penalty for failing to liquidate the full position:

ψ(xT)=A xT2,A→∞\psi(x_T) = A \, x_T^2, \quad A \to \inftyψ(xT​)=AxT2​,A→∞
(17)

which forces xT≈0x_T \approx 0xT​≈0 in the limit. The terminal condition thus encodes the hard constraint that the position must be closed at the end of the trading horizon. In practice, a large but finite AAA corresponds to the cost of liquidating any residual at market at time TTT.

Connection to the Feynman–Kac theorem¶

Once the optimal control u∗(t,x)u^*(t, x)u∗(t,x) is substituted back into the HJB equation, the resulting PDE is linear in JJJ and takes the form covered by the Feynman–Kac theorem (chapter Stochastic Calculus, section The Feynman - Kac Theorem):

∂J∂t+μ∗(x,t)∂J∂x+12σ2(x,t)∂2J∂x2−r J+c∗(t,x)=0\frac{\partial J}{\partial t} + \mu^*(x, t) \frac{\partial J}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(x,t) \frac{\partial^2 J}{\partial x^2} - r \, J + c^*(t, x) = 0∂t∂J​+μ∗(x,t)∂x∂J​+21​σ2(x,t)∂x2∂2J​−rJ+c∗(t,x)=0
(18)

where μ∗=μ(x,u∗(t,x),t)\mu^* = \mu(x, u^*(t,x), t)μ∗=μ(x,u∗(t,x),t) and c∗=c(t,x,u∗(t,x))c^* = c(t, x, u^*(t,x))c∗=c(t,x,u∗(t,x)) are the optimal drift and cost. The Feynman–Kac theorem then identifies J(t,x)J(t, x)J(t,x) with the expected discounted cost under the optimal dynamics:

J(t,x)=E[∫tTe−r(s−t)c∗(s,Xs) ds+e−r(T−t)ψ(XT) ∣ Xt=x]J(t, x) = \mathbb{E}\left[\int_t^T e^{-r(s-t)} c^*(s, X_s) \, ds + e^{-r(T-t)}\psi(X_T) \,\Bigg|\, X_t = x\right]J(t,x)=E[∫tT​e−r(s−t)c∗(s,Xs​)ds+e−r(T−t)ψ(XT​)∣∣​Xt​=x]
(19)

This confirms the probabilistic interpretation of the value function and provides a Monte Carlo method for computing JJJ numerically when the PDE is not analytically tractable.

The variational approach¶

Calculus of variations¶

The calculus of variations studies functionals — real-valued functions whose argument is itself a function — and asks: for what function is a given functional minimised or maximised? In the control problems of interest, the functional is the expected total cost and the unknown is the trajectory of the state variable.

Consider minimising the functional

F[x]=∫0TL(t,xt,x˙t) dt\mathcal{F}[x] = \int_0^T L(t, x_t, \dot{x}_t) \, dtF[x]=∫0T​L(t,xt​,x˙t​)dt
(20)

over smooth trajectories x:[0,T]→Rx: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}x:[0,T]→R subject to fixed boundary conditions x(0)=x0x(0) = x_0x(0)=x0​ and x(T)=xTx(T) = x_Tx(T)=xT​. The integrand L(t,x,x˙)L(t, x, \dot{x})L(t,x,x˙) is called the Lagrangian. The trajectory x∗x^*x∗ that extremises F\mathcal{F}F satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation:

∂L∂x−ddt∂L∂x˙=0\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} = 0∂x∂L​−dtd​∂x˙∂L​=0
(21)

This is a second-order ordinary differential equation for xtx_txt​, solved subject to the two boundary conditions.

The variational approach applies directly to stochastic optimal control problems in which the noise enters the cost functional only through the trajectory of the state — not through the control variable itself. This occurs in the Almgren–Chriss model, where:

  • the expected implementation shortfall depends deterministically on the trajectory {xt}\{x_t\}{xt​},

  • the variance of implementation shortfall depends deterministically on {xt}\{x_t\}{xt​},

  • the mean–variance objective is therefore a deterministic functional of the state trajectory.

In such cases, the stochastic optimisation reduces to a deterministic variational problem.

Euler–Lagrange equation for execution¶

In the Almgren–Chriss model (derived in detail in chapter Optimal Execution Theory), the Lagrangian takes the form

L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2L(x, \dot{x}) = \eta \dot{x}^2 + \lambda \sigma^2 x^2L(x,x˙)=ηx˙2+λσ2x2
(22)

where η>0\eta > 0η>0 is the temporary market impact coefficient, σ\sigmaσ is the price volatility, and λ≥0\lambda \geq 0λ≥0 is the risk-aversion parameter. The Euler–Lagrange equation gives:

∂L∂x−ddt∂L∂x˙=2λσ2x−2ηx¨=0\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} = 2\lambda\sigma^2 x - 2\eta \ddot{x} = 0∂x∂L​−dtd​∂x˙∂L​=2λσ2x−2ηx¨=0
(23)

equivalently,

x¨=κ2x,κ≡λσ2η\ddot{x} = \kappa^2 x, \quad \kappa \equiv \sqrt{\frac{\lambda \sigma^2}{\eta}}x¨=κ2x,κ≡ηλσ2​​
(24)

This is a second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients. The general solution is:

xt=Asinh⁡(κt)+Bcosh⁡(κt)x_t = A \sinh(\kappa t) + B \cosh(\kappa t)xt​=Asinh(κt)+Bcosh(κt)
(25)

where AAA and BBB are determined by the boundary conditions x0=Xx_0 = Xx0​=X (initial inventory) and xT=0x_T = 0xT​=0 (complete liquidation). This yields the unique optimal trajectory:

xt∗=X sinh⁡(κ(T−t))sinh⁡(κT)x_t^* = X \, \frac{\sinh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}xt∗​=Xsinh(κT)sinh(κ(T−t))​
(26)

The parameter κ\kappaκ controls the shape of the trajectory: for κ→0\kappa \to 0κ→0 (risk-neutral, λ→0\lambda \to 0λ→0), the trajectory reduces to a linear decrease xt∗=X(1−t/T)x_t^* = X(1 - t/T)xt∗​=X(1−t/T) — the TWAP schedule. For large κ\kappaκ (highly risk-averse), the trajectory front-loads aggressively, liquidating most of the position early and leaving only a small residual towards the end.

Hyperbolic solution structure¶

The hyperbolic sine and cosine functions that appear in the solution have a natural interpretation. Define the half-life τ∗=1/κ\tau^* = 1/\kappaτ∗=1/κ as the characteristic time over which the optimal strategy departs significantly from the risk-neutral uniform schedule. For T≪τ∗T \ll \tau^*T≪τ∗ (short horizon relative to the risk-aversion scale), the solution is approximately linear: xt∗≈X(1−t/T)x_t^* \approx X(1 - t/T)xt∗​≈X(1−t/T). For T≫τ∗T \gg \tau^*T≫τ∗, the solution approximates an exponential decay in the early portion, then abruptly falls to zero near TTT.

The trading rate is

vt∗=−x˙t∗=κX cosh⁡(κ(T−t))sinh⁡(κT)v_t^* = -\dot{x}_t^* = \kappa X \, \frac{\cosh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}vt∗​=−x˙t∗​=κXsinh(κT)cosh(κ(T−t))​
(27)

This is a decreasing function of time: the optimal strategy sells most aggressively at time t=0t = 0t=0 and slows down as the horizon approaches — front-loading to reduce exposure to price risk from holding a large unexecuted inventory, at the cost of higher early market impact.

Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control¶

Problem setup¶

Linear–Quadratic Stochastic Control (LQSC) is a class of stochastic control problems in which:

  • the state dynamics are linear in the state and control,

  • the cost functional is quadratic in the state and control,

  • the noise is Gaussian (additive, independent of state and control).

These three properties together guarantee that the value function is quadratic in the state, the optimal control is affine (linear plus a constant) in the state, and the optimal gains satisfy a backwards Riccati equation — a system of ODEs or recursions that can be solved analytically or efficiently numerically.

In discrete time, the LQSC problem is:

min⁡{uk}E[∑k=0N−1(xkTQkxk+ukTRkuk+2qkTxk+2rkTuk)+xNTPNxN+2pNTxN]\min_{\{u_k\}} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left(x_k^T Q_k x_k + u_k^T R_k u_k + 2 q_k^T x_k + 2 r_k^T u_k\right) + x_N^T P_N x_N + 2 p_N^T x_N\right]{uk​}min​E[k=0∑N−1​(xkT​Qk​xk​+ukT​Rk​uk​+2qkT​xk​+2rkT​uk​)+xNT​PN​xN​+2pNT​xN​]
(28)

subject to the linear dynamics

xk+1=Akxk+Bkuk+ck+wkx_{k+1} = A_k x_k + B_k u_k + c_k + w_kxk+1​=Ak​xk​+Bk​uk​+ck​+wk​
(29)

where xk∈Rnx_k \in \mathbb{R}^nxk​∈Rn is the state, uk∈Rmu_k \in \mathbb{R}^muk​∈Rm is the control, wk∼N(0,Wk)w_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W_k)wk​∼N(0,Wk​) is a Gaussian disturbance independent of xkx_kxk​ and uku_kuk​, Ak∈Rn×nA_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Ak​∈Rn×n, Bk∈Rn×mB_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}Bk​∈Rn×m, Qk⪰0Q_k \succeq 0Qk​⪰0, Rk≻0R_k \succ 0Rk​≻0, and PN⪰0P_N \succeq 0PN​⪰0.

The quadratic value function ansatz¶

The key observation is that the Bellman equation preserves the quadratic structure of the value function. We postulate:

Vk(x)=xTPkx+2pkTx+qkV_k(x) = x^T P_k x + 2 p_k^T x + q_kVk​(x)=xTPk​x+2pkT​x+qk​
(30)

and verify that this form is consistent with the Bellman equation. Substituting the ansatz into the Bellman equation and minimising over uku_kuk​ (which is unconstrained for simplicity):

The minimand is:

xTQkx+2qkTx+uTRku+2rkTu+(Akx+Bku+ck)TPk+1(Akx+Bku+ck)+…x^T Q_k x + 2q_k^T x + u^T R_k u + 2r_k^T u + (A_k x + B_k u + c_k)^T P_{k+1}(A_k x + B_k u + c_k) + \ldotsxTQk​x+2qkT​x+uTRk​u+2rkT​u+(Ak​x+Bk​u+ck​)TPk+1​(Ak​x+Bk​u+ck​)+…
(31)

Taking the derivative with respect to uuu and setting to zero:

2Rku+2BkTPk+1(Akx+Bku+ck)+2(rk+BkTpk+1)=02 R_k u + 2 B_k^T P_{k+1}(A_k x + B_k u + c_k) + 2(r_k + B_k^T p_{k+1}) = 02Rk​u+2BkT​Pk+1​(Ak​x+Bk​u+ck​)+2(rk​+BkT​pk+1​)=0
(32)

Solving for the optimal control:

uk∗=Kkxk+ℓk\boxed{u_k^* = K_k x_k + \ell_k}uk∗​=Kk​xk​+ℓk​​
(33)

where

Kk=−(Rk+BkTPk+1Bk)−1BkTPk+1AkK_k = -(R_k + B_k^T P_{k+1} B_k)^{-1} B_k^T P_{k+1} A_kKk​=−(Rk​+BkT​Pk+1​Bk​)−1BkT​Pk+1​Ak​
(34)
ℓk=−(Rk+BkTPk+1Bk)−1(BkTPk+1ck+BkTpk+1+rk)\ell_k = -(R_k + B_k^T P_{k+1} B_k)^{-1}(B_k^T P_{k+1} c_k + B_k^T p_{k+1} + r_k)ℓk​=−(Rk​+BkT​Pk+1​Bk​)−1(BkT​Pk+1​ck​+BkT​pk+1​+rk​)
(35)

The optimal control is affine in the state: a linear feedback term KkxkK_k x_kKk​xk​ plus a constant correction ℓk\ell_kℓk​. The feedback gain KkK_kKk​ depends only on the matrices of the problem, not on the realisation of noise.

Riccati equations¶

Substituting the optimal control back into the Bellman equation yields recursions for the coefficients PkP_kPk​, pkp_kpk​, qkq_kqk​, which are the matrix Riccati equations:

Pk=Qk+AkTPk+1Ak−AkTPk+1Bk(Rk+BkTPk+1Bk)−1BkTPk+1Ak\boxed{P_k = Q_k + A_k^T P_{k+1} A_k - A_k^T P_{k+1} B_k (R_k + B_k^T P_{k+1} B_k)^{-1} B_k^T P_{k+1} A_k}Pk​=Qk​+AkT​Pk+1​Ak​−AkT​Pk+1​Bk​(Rk​+BkT​Pk+1​Bk​)−1BkT​Pk+1​Ak​​
(36)
pk=qk+AkTpk+1−AkTPk+1Bk(Rk+BkTPk+1Bk)−1(BkTpk+1+rk)+AkTPk+1ckp_k = q_k + A_k^T p_{k+1} - A_k^T P_{k+1} B_k (R_k + B_k^T P_{k+1} B_k)^{-1}(B_k^T p_{k+1} + r_k) + A_k^T P_{k+1} c_kpk​=qk​+AkT​pk+1​−AkT​Pk+1​Bk​(Rk​+BkT​Pk+1​Bk​)−1(BkT​pk+1​+rk​)+AkT​Pk+1​ck​
(37)

with terminal conditions PNP_NPN​ and pNp_NpN​ given. The noise term wkw_kwk​ contributes only to the scalar qkq_kqk​, not to PkP_kPk​ or pkp_kpk​: this is the certainty equivalence property of LQSC — the optimal feedback gains are identical to those of the deterministic version of the problem (obtained by setting wk=0w_k = 0wk​=0), and noise only increases the expected cost.

The computational cost of the Riccati recursion is O(Nn3)O(Nn^3)O(Nn3) (matrix inversions at each of NNN steps for nnn-dimensional state), which is tractable for the problem sizes arising in execution (state dimension 2–4, horizon NNN = 20–400 time bins).

Scalar LQSC: the Riccati recursion in closed form¶

For the scalar case (n=m=1n = m = 1n=m=1, Ak=aA_k = aAk​=a, Bk=bB_k = bBk​=b, Qk=qQ_k = qQk​=q, Rk=rR_k = rRk​=r), the Riccati recursion simplifies to:

Pk=q+a2Pk+1−a2b2Pk+12r+b2Pk+1P_k = q + a^2 P_{k+1} - \frac{a^2 b^2 P_{k+1}^2}{r + b^2 P_{k+1}}Pk​=q+a2Pk+1​−r+b2Pk+1​a2b2Pk+12​​
(38)

This can be written as:

Pk=q+a2rPk+1r+b2Pk+1P_k = q + \frac{a^2 r P_{k+1}}{r + b^2 P_{k+1}}Pk​=q+r+b2Pk+1​a2rPk+1​​
(39)

which is a scalar nonlinear recursion that can be evaluated numerically with PNP_NPN​ as the terminal condition. For the stationary case (aaa, bbb, qqq, rrr constant), the recursion converges as N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞ to the fixed point of the algebraic Riccati equation P∗=q+a2rP∗/(r+b2P∗)P^* = q + a^2 r P^* / (r + b^2 P^*)P∗=q+a2rP∗/(r+b2P∗).

Continuous-time LQSC¶

In continuous time, the LQSC problem is:

min⁡{ut}E[∫0T(xtTQtxt+utTRtut)dt+xTTPTxT]\min_{\{u_t\}} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T \left(x_t^T Q_t x_t + u_t^T R_t u_t\right) dt + x_T^T P_T x_T\right]{ut​}min​E[∫0T​(xtT​Qt​xt​+utT​Rt​ut​)dt+xTT​PT​xT​]
(40)

subject to dXt=(AtXt+Btut) dt+Σt dWtdX_t = (A_t X_t + B_t u_t) \, dt + \Sigma_t \, dW_tdXt​=(At​Xt​+Bt​ut​)dt+Σt​dWt​. The HJB equation is:

−P˙t=Qt+AtTPt+PtAt−PtBtRt−1BtTPt-\dot{P}_t = Q_t + A_t^T P_t + P_t A_t - P_t B_t R_t^{-1} B_t^T P_t−P˙t​=Qt​+AtT​Pt​+Pt​At​−Pt​Bt​Rt−1​BtT​Pt​
(41)

with terminal condition PTP_TPT​ (matrix-valued). This is the continuous-time matrix Riccati ODE. The optimal control is ut∗=−Rt−1BtTPtxtu_t^* = -R_t^{-1} B_t^T P_t x_tut∗​=−Rt−1​BtT​Pt​xt​ — a linear feedback policy with time-varying gain Kt=−Rt−1BtTPtK_t = -R_t^{-1} B_t^T P_tKt​=−Rt−1​BtT​Pt​. The certainty-equivalence property holds: the Riccati ODE does not depend on the noise covariance Σt\Sigma_tΣt​, which affects only the expected cost, not the optimal gains.

Structured extensions for execution problems¶

Both the VWAP execution problem and the market making problem introduce additional structure: the state vector includes not only the inventory but also a stochastic auxiliary state (the cumulative market volume for VWAP, or the asset price for market making) that is not directly controlled. The LQSC framework handles this naturally by extending the state vector and setting the corresponding control gain to zero.

More precisely, in the VWAP problem (chapter Optimal Execution Theory), the state is xk=(Qk,Vk)Tx_k = (Q_k, V_k)^Txk​=(Qk​,Vk​)T where QkQ_kQk​ is the cumulative order executed and VkV_kVk​ is the cumulative market volume. The market volume VkV_kVk​ evolves stochastically and independently of the control qkq_kqk​ (shares executed in bin kkk). The Riccati recursion then produces gains Kk=(Kk,1,Kk,2)K_k = (K_{k,1}, K_{k,2})Kk​=(Kk,1​,Kk,2​) where Kk,1K_{k,1}Kk,1​ governs feedback on the execution shortfall and Kk,2K_{k,2}Kk,2​ governs adaptation to observed volume. This adaptive structure is what makes the dynamic VWAP strategy superior to its static counterpart.
